title: Peripartum Cardiomyopathy
keywords: diagnosis requires heart failure developing in the last month of pregnancy through 5 months postpartum, an ejection fraction under 45 percent, and no other identifiable cause, four criteria not just a low EF found incidentally postpartum

easy to misattribute dyspnea/edema/fatigue in late pregnancy or early postpartum to normal pregnancy physiology, a real and dangerous diagnostic delay pattern, have a lower threshold for an echo in this population than you would otherwise

bromocriptine added to standard heart failure therapy improves LV function/remodeling in the current evidence base, mechanism is stopping prolactin, whose cleaved fragment is implicated in the disease process, this is not yet universal standard of care everywhere
standard heart failure medications need pregnancy/lactation-safe substitutions, ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated in pregnancy, know which agents are safe to use instead
anticoagulation is a real consideration given the elevated thromboembolic risk with a severely reduced EF in the peripartum period, not an afterthought
sources: Bauersachs J, et al. Pathophysiology, diagnosis and management of peripartum cardiomyopathy: a position statement from the ESC Study Group. Eur J Heart Fail. 2019;21(7):827-843.
Adamu J, et al. Bromocriptine in peripartum cardiomyopathy: A meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis. ESC Heart Fail. 2025.
Arany Z, Elkayam U. Peripartum Cardiomyopathy. Circulation. 2016;133(14):1397-1409.

changelog.change: Initial entry — a genuine content gap (Content audit 2026-09-15, fresh-look Batch 8). Previously only a bare tag mention inside heart-failure-continuum with no dedicated content — this module supplies the PPCM-specific diagnostic criteria and pregnancy/lactation-safe management nuances that general heart failure content doesn't address.

summary: Peripartum cardiomyopathy is easy to misattribute to normal late-pregnancy physiology — dyspnea, edema, and fatigue overlap heavily with a normal pregnancy — so a lower threshold for an echo in this population matters, and diagnosis requires the specific combination of heart failure timing, EF under 45%, and no other identifiable cause, not just an incidentally low EF found postpartum.
whyThisMatters: The classic PPCM symptoms overlap so heavily with expected late-pregnancy and early-postpartum physiology that real diagnostic delay is a documented pattern — recognizing when dyspnea/edema/fatigue has crossed from 'normal pregnancy' into 'possible heart failure' territory, and knowing which standard heart failure medications are actually safe in pregnancy/lactation, are the two places this diagnosis most commonly goes wrong.
clinicalTakeaway: Diagnostic criteria (all four required): heart failure developing in the last month of pregnancy through 5 months postpartum; LV ejection fraction under 45% (with or without LV dilatation); no other identifiable cause of heart failure; no recognizable heart disease before the last month of pregnancy. Have a genuinely lower threshold for obtaining an echocardiogram in a peripartum patient with dyspnea, edema, or fatigue that seems more than expected for normal pregnancy — diagnostic delay from misattributing these symptoms to pregnancy itself is a real, documented pattern. Use pregnancy/lactation-safe heart failure medications — ACE inhibitors and ARBs are CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy (teratogenic), substitute hydralazine/nitrates for afterload reduction antepartum, with ACE-I/ARB reintroduction typically reasonable postpartum depending on lactation plans and specific agent. Bromocriptine added to standard heart failure therapy has current evidence (including a 2025 meta-analysis) supporting improved LV function/remodeling, based on stopping prolactin (a cleaved prolactin fragment is implicated in the disease's pathophysiology) — discuss with cardiology/maternal-fetal medicine as this isn't yet universal standard of care everywhere. Consider anticoagulation given elevated thromboembolic risk with a severely reduced EF in the peripartum period.

body.text: Diagnostic criteria — four required, not just a low EF

items: Development of heart failure in the LAST MONTH of pregnancy through 5 MONTHS POSTPARTUM.
Left ventricular ejection fraction under 45% (some sources also reference fractional shortening under 30% and/or LV end-diastolic dimension criteria), with or without LV dilatation.
Absence of an identifiable alternative cause of heart failure.
No recognizable heart disease before the last month of pregnancy.

body.text: All four criteria matter — an incidentally discovered low ejection fraction outside this specific timing window, or in a patient with pre-existing heart disease, is NOT peripartum cardiomyopathy by definition, even if it looks superficially similar. The timing criterion in particular is what distinguishes PPCM from other causes of cardiomyopathy discovered around the time of pregnancy.
Recognition — don't misattribute symptoms to normal pregnancy

Dyspnea, lower extremity edema, and fatigue are all common in normal late pregnancy and the early postpartum period, which makes PPCM genuinely easy to miss or delay diagnosing — these same symptoms are the presenting complaints of heart failure. Red flags that should lower the threshold for echocardiography: symptoms that are more severe or more rapidly progressive than typical for the patient's gestational stage, orthopnea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (less typical of normal pregnancy physiology), or new-onset symptoms particularly in the immediate postpartum period (when normal pregnancy-related dyspnea would be expected to be improving, not worsening).

items: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are CONTRAINDICATED during pregnancy (teratogenic) — use hydralazine and nitrates for afterload reduction antepartum instead. Postpartum, ACE-I/ARB use can typically be reconsidered, with specific agent choice informed by lactation plans (some agents are considered more compatible with breastfeeding than others).
Beta-blockers (e.g. carvedilol, metoprolol succinate) are generally continued/used as in standard heart failure management, with appropriate pregnancy-category considerations per agent.
Diuretics are used for volume management as in standard heart failure care.

BROMOCRIPTINE as an adjunct to standard heart failure therapy: current evidence, including a 2025 meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis, supports improved LV functional recovery and remodeling with bromocriptine added to standard care, based on the mechanism of suppressing prolactin (a cleaved 16-kDa prolactin fragment has been implicated as pathogenic in PPCM). This is a genuine, evolving area of practice — not yet universal standard of care in every center — and should be discussed with cardiology/maternal-fetal medicine rather than started unilaterally.

Anticoagulation: consider given the elevated thromboembolic risk that accompanies a severely reduced ejection fraction in the peripartum period specifically (a time of baseline hypercoagulability) — this is a real management consideration, not an afterthought, though the specific threshold/regimen is a specialist-guided decision.

body.text: A substantial proportion of patients recover meaningful LV function, though recovery is not universal and some progress to chronic heart failure. Future pregnancy carries a real risk of PPCM recurrence, particularly in patients whose LV function has not fully recovered — this is an important counseling point for a patient of reproductive age who has had PPCM, best addressed collaboratively with cardiology and maternal-fetal medicine before a subsequent pregnancy is attempted.
